claims.text: The material under study is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
Degradation of this alloy during elevated-temperature gas exposure is primarily governed by the formation and evolution of surface oxide scales.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Ti oxidize rapidly.
Oxidation of Al and Ti produces a thick, potentially porous mixed-oxide scale.
The thick mixed-oxide scale disrupts grain-boundary integrity.
Limited oxide formation under reducing conditions preserves the integrity of the fcc matrix.
The as-printed alloy has a fine, homogeneous fcc microstructure.
The as-printed alloy has minimal surface oxidation.
Oxide-scale thickness, porosity, and adhesion modulate grain-boundary integrity in the fcc matrix.
A porous or poorly adherent oxide scale causes grain-boundary embrittlement and microstructural degradation.
Reducing atmospheres produce a thinner, more protective oxide layer than oxidizing atmospheres.
The thinner oxide formed under reducing conditions preserves matrix cohesion and mechanical properties.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a thicker, less adherent, and more porous oxide scale than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will cause larger decreases in hardness and tensile strength than reducing exposure.
The proposed behavior applies near 900 °C under clearly defined oxidizing or reducing gas compositions.
Temperatures far from 900 °C or mixed-gas environments may produce different degradation behavior.
Thermal exposure may introduce contributions from minor phase transformations.
Comparable oxide scales and mechanical degradation in the oxidizing and reducing environments, or absence of a correlation between scale formation and degradation, would falsify the hypothesis.
